mn101:2.5: Note the wrong view of many people these days who regard everything experienced as the result of past kamma. If this were true, no way out (to Nibbāna) would be possible.
mn101:4.3: ‘Do you know that you existed in the past, and not that you did not exist?’
mn101:6.1: For the two ‘sequels’ see Sutta 95, para. 14.
mn101:7.21: P.T.S. Ed. here has abbyaheyya but abbaheyya in the parallel passage at M.ii, 257; the Siamese readings differ, and neither form is in the P.T.S. Dict. The application of this simile is that the wounded man remembers all the painful details about his wound, while the Jains only assume that they were ‘wounded’ (by evil kammas) in the past, but remember nothing.
mn101:10.5: This refers to Nātaputta’s teaching ‘you have done evil kammas in the past’—have the Nigaṇṭhas examined his teaching to find out whether it is factual or not in the light of these five things? There is no ‘reasonable defence’ among them, because they have accepted the teaching instead of critically examining it.
mn101:11.4: These five are a touchstone for one’s views. They are introduced here since the Jains have said that Nātaputta’s teaching was their preference (the second of the five) and to their liking (the last of the five).
mn101:13.1: It is obvious that the pain experienced originates not from the past but from present actions (such as continuous exertion).
mn101:18.1: The point of this and the following exchange is that the fruits of kamma which will be experienced by an old person cannot, however one strives, be experienced when young, and the reverse; such kinds of kamma only ripen when conditions (of age, in this case) are fulfilled.
mn101:22.7: Saṅgatibhāva, here rendered ‘circumstance’: elsewhere (Sutta 60) rendered ‘coincidence’. ‘Destiny’ is a completely determined state about which beings can do nothing.
mn101:22.9: Abhijāti—class of origin: also mentioned in Sutta 60, and explained at D. 2.
mn101:23.2: A bhikkhu, unlike the Nigaṇṭhas, does not add pain to his body such that he cannot handle the situation.
mn101:27.4: For instance, in the austere practices (having only three robes, living at the root of a tree, eating once a day, never lying down, and so on); see Vis. Ch. II. Fasting for a few days, or not sleeping at night, can also be included here, as can the pain from long stretches of sitting and walking meditation.
